conceptTag: Design ticket prices for a museum
readerTitle: Same paintings, different prices: pricing a museum ticket
caseNote: 가상 사례 (시립 미술관, 사내 영상팀, 타일 유통업체) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 티켓 가격 하나를 정하는 일은 '누가' 내는가와 '언제' 오는가라는 두 개의 레버를 함께 설계하는 일이다.
misconception: 방문객을 늘리려면 모두에게 가격을 낮추면 된다. 같은 상품에는 누구에게나 같은 가격을 받아야 공정하다.

sources.text: 가격 차별(price discrimination)과 시간대별 가격(dynamic pricing)에 대한 표준 경제학 개념

factChecks.note: 가상 수치 계산 확인: $20에서 $15로 내리면 매출을 유지하려면 방문객이 20 ÷ 15 = 1.33배, 즉 약 33% 늘어야 합니다(방문객 한 명당 추가 비용은 거의 없다고 가정).
softwareNote의 '클라우드 업체가 남는 서버 용량을 더 싸게 판다'는 일반적 설명입니다. 특정 기업명이나 할인율은 쓰지 않았습니다. 게시 전 표현이 과하지 않은지 확인하세요.
실제 미술관의 요금 정책(자율 기부 입장, 거주자 할인 등)은 특정 기관 사례로 쓰지 않았습니다. 실제 사례를 추가하려면 해당 기관 공식 자료로 확인해야 합니다.

cards.title: Same paintings, different prices: pricing a museum ticket
body: A city museum charges $20 a ticket. On Saturdays the line wraps around the block by noon. On Tuesdays the guards outnumber the visitors.
The paintings are the same both days. The single price is the problem.

image.label: Museum gallery split between a crowded Saturday and an empty Tuesday
image.brief: 한 미술관 전시실을 좌우로 나눈 일러스트. 왼쪽은 'Saturday' 사람으로 꽉 찬 모습, 오른쪽은 'Tuesday' 경비원 한 명만 서 있는 텅 빈 모습. 입구에 '$20' 가격판 하나. 실제 미술관 이름이나 로고, 실존 명화는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: The board wants more visitors.
body: You run the museum. The board wants more students and local families to visit, without losing ticket revenue.
Which move do you make first?

options.text: Cut the ticket to $15 for everyone
options.feedback: Every visitor who would gladly pay $20 now pays $15. You'd need about 33% more visitors just to stand still.

options.text: Keep $20, and charge students and seniors $10 with ID
options.feedback: This is **price discrimination**: a lower price for the groups you want, held apart by an ID check. Full-price visitors still pay full price.

options.text: Make the first Sunday of each month free for everyone
options.feedback: It draws a crowd, but many free visitors would have paid, and it adds people to a weekend that's already full.

cards.title: Price discrimination needs a fence.
body: **Price discrimination** means charging different customers different prices for the same thing, based on what each group is willing or able to pay.

It only works with a **fence**: a rule that separates the groups and that people can't easily cross. A student card, a local address, a school group booking. Without a fence, everyone claims the discount and you're back to option A.

image.label: Ticket desk with two lanes separated by an ID check
image.brief: 매표소 앞에 두 줄. 한 줄은 'Adult $20', 다른 줄은 'Student / Senior $10'. 두 줄 사이에 낮은 울타리와 'Show ID' 표지판. 단순하고 밝은 플랫 일러스트.

cards.title: Price the day, not just the person.
body: Saturdays sell out. Tuesdays don't. Many visitors are flexible, so a different price by day moves some of them. This is a simple form of **dynamic pricing**: price follows demand over time.

breakdown.label: Weekend adult
breakdown.detail: For those who want the busy day

cards.callout: The schedule is posted in advance, so nobody is surprised at the door.
cards.softwareNote: Software uses both levers too: student and nonprofit plans behind a verification fence, and cloud providers selling spare server capacity more cheaply when demand is low.

cards.title: Fair matters more than clever.
body: A museum isn't a concert. If weekend prices climb too high, families who can only come on Saturdays feel shut out, and the mission suffers.
Prices that change hour by hour feel like gouging. A posted weekday and weekend price feels fair.
Fences cost money too. Checking every ID slows the line. Keep the rules few and easy to explain.

cards.eyebrow: Try it · team inside a company
cards.title: Everyone wants the video team at once.
body: Your company's in-house video team charges other departments $1,500 per shoot day. Every department books the last two weeks of each quarter. The first weeks sit empty, and the team is burning out.

options.text: Charge more for end-of-quarter days and less for early-quarter days
options.feedback: This is **dynamic pricing** by time. Departments with flexible deadlines move early, and the rush shrinks without a ban.

options.text: Keep the rate and book first come, first served
options.feedback: It feels fair, but nothing nudges anyone to move. The crunch stays, and the fastest bookers win.

options.text: Raise the rate on every day
options.feedback: Demand falls all year, including in the weeks that were already empty. The peak barely changes.

cards.title: Contractors and homeowners at one counter.
body: You run a tile and flooring distributor. Contractors buy every week and compare prices hard. Homeowners buy once. Both ask for a discount at the counter.

options.text: Give the discount to anyone who asks
options.feedback: A fence anyone can cross isn't a fence. Soon nobody pays list price, and the discount becomes your real price.

options.text: Trade prices for registered contractor accounts, list price for walk-ins
options.feedback: **Price discrimination** with a clear fence: the account. You keep frequent buyers loyal and still earn full price from one-time shoppers.
Simple and easy to defend, but contractors may drift to cheaper rivals, and homeowners pay less than they would have.

cards.title: Ask who pays, and when.
body: Two ideas did the work here. **Price discrimination**: different prices for different groups, held apart by a fence. **Dynamic pricing**: different prices for different times, so flexible customers fill the quiet hours.
**Try it today:** write down your busiest and quietest times, and one group who would buy more at a lower price. What simple fence would keep that price for them alone?
